analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health insurance program covering everyone in America, replacing private health insurance for medically necessary care.
analysis.headline: The Medicare-for-all bill, backed by 78 House members, was sent to four House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor consideration before Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 676 would have replaced private health insurance with a single government-run program covering everyone living in the United States. It covered all medically necessary care — doctor visits, hospital stays, prescription drugs, dental, vision, mental health, and long-term care — with no deductibles, copays, or coinsurance [S2][S3]. Private insurers could no longer sell coverage duplicating those benefits, for-profit hospitals would have had to convert to nonprofit status over 15 years, and drug prices would be negotiated centrally with bulk purchasing [S2][S3]. The program would be funded by redirecting existing federal health spending, cutting paperwork, raising income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a payroll tax, and a small tax on stock and bond transactions [S2][S3]. It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, sent to their subcommittees, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the roughly 45 million uninsured Americans at the time would have gained full coverage, and everyone else would have traded premiums, deductibles, copays, and network restrictions for a government card covering all medically necessary care with no out-of-pocket costs [S2][S3]. People with pre-existing conditions would no longer face denial or price discrimination, and patients would keep free choice of any participating doctor or hospital [S3]. Displaced insurance clerical workers would get retraining priority [S3]. Higher earners and owners of financial assets would pay more through the top-5% income tax increase, the payroll tax, and the stock and bond transaction tax [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone living in the United States

how_it_helps.text: Every person living in the United States would receive a national health insurance card covering all medically necessary care, including doctor visits, hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, vision, mental health, substance abuse treatment, chiropractic, and long-term care [S2][S3 Sec. 101-102].

No deductibles, copayments, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing would be charged for covered benefits, ending out-of-pocket costs that today cause people to skip care or face medical debt [S2][S3 Sec. 102(c)].

Coverage would be portable: benefits usable with any licensed clinician anywhere in the country, ending network restrictions, and patients would have free choice of participating doctors and hospitals [S2][S3 Sec. 102(b), 103(d)].

The program would be paid for by reducing paperwork, bulk-purchasing medications, redirecting existing federal health spending, raising income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a modest payroll tax, and a small tax on stock and bond transactions [S2][S3 Sec. 211].
Clerical and administrative workers whose insurance and billing jobs disappear would get first priority in retraining and job placement in the new system [S3 Sec. 303(e)].
The bill directs the program to reduce health disparities by race, ethnicity, income, and region, and to favor home- and community-based long-term care over institutional care [S3 Sec. 203(d), 403].

analysis.who_pays: The top 5% of income earners would face higher income taxes; all workers and employers would pay a modest new payroll tax; and investors would pay a small tax on stock and bond transactions [S2][S3]. Private health insurers would lose the core of their business since duplicating coverage would be unlawful [S2][S3]. Brand-name drug makers would face centrally negotiated prices and bulk purchasing [S2][S3]. For-profit hospitals and other investor-owned providers would have to convert to nonprofit status over 15 years, compensated only for appraised property and equipment, not lost profits [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy households, private insurers, drug makers

drawbacks.text: Funding would require new taxes on nearly everyone, not just the wealthy: a payroll tax on top of higher income taxes on the top 5% of earners and a new tax on stock and bond transactions [S2][S3 Sec. 211].

The bill left key dollar amounts unspecified, authorizing 'such sums as may be necessary' and setting tax rates through the annual appropriations process, so the real cost and tax burden would be decided later without a firm number attached [S3 Sec. 211].
Taxpayers would fund the purchase of investor-owned health facilities at appraised value over 15 years through Treasury bonds, a large conversion cost on top of program expenses [S3 Sec. 103].

Tens of thousands of insurance-company and billing clerical workers would see their jobs eliminated; the bill offers them retraining and job-placement priority but no guarantee of comparable employment [S3 Sec. 303(e)].

Converting hospitals to fixed global budgets and banning balance billing creates a real risk that the annual budget negotiations could underpay providers, with patients unable to buy supplementary coverage for any medically necessary service [S3 Sec. 104].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gains were large: everyone in the country would have gotten comprehensive coverage with no deductibles or copays, funded partly by taxing the top 5% of earners, and administrative savings and bulk drug purchasing would offset some costs [S2][S3]. The costs were real and serious: the new payroll, income, and financial-transaction taxes would replace premiums for everyone, the exact tax rates were left to annual appropriations, the 15-year buyout of investor-owned facilities was a large expense, and millions of insurance and billing jobs would shrink, with retraining offered but not guaranteed [S3]. Whether the global-budget payment model could control costs without causing wait times or underpayment of providers was untested at this scale. An honest weighing: the bill proposed the largest health system redesign in American history with substantial promised savings and substantial unquantified costs, and it never received a committee hearing or a Congressional Budget Office analysis that would have tested either side of that ledger [S5].

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to four committees and then to their health subcommittees, and no committee ever took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced H.R. 676 on February 8, 2005, with Reps. Kucinich, McDermott, and Christensen as original sponsors [S1][S3][S5].
The same day, the House referred it to four committees at once: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Natural Resources, and Veterans' Affairs [S5].
Within weeks in February 2005, it was referred to the health subcommittees of those committees; no markup, hearing, or committee vote on the bill appears in the action history [S5].
Over the next two years, 78 House members signed on as cosponsors, 77 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].
The only other recorded action was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on May 2, 2006 [S5].
The bill expired on January 3, 2007, when the 109th Congress ended, with no vote ever taken in the House or Senate [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and for-profit hospitals and providers, all of which kept the existing insurance-based system and its revenue untouched, along with the committee chairs who preserved the status quo without ever having to vote against the bill on its merits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, drug makers, for-profit hospitals

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in February 2005 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor in May 2006; the bill never advanced past committee referral.

for.name: 77 of 201 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — roughly a third of the House Democratic caucus — giving it substantial formal support but no committee action.

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the chamber's sole Independent.

against.name: Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the first-listed committee of referral; the record shows no markup, hearing, or committee vote on H.R. 676 during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee with jurisdiction over the bill's taxes and Medicare financing; no action on the bill appears in the record.

against.name: Steve Buyer
against.what_they_did: Chaired one of the four committees of referral; no action on the bill appears in the record.

against.name: Private health insurance industry
against.role: Health insurers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed single-payer proposals that would eliminate private coverage for medically necessary care.

sides.party_line_note: All 78 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican committee chairs took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to sell coverage duplicating the program's benefits, which are far broader than most current plans, eliminating the industry's core business [S2][S3 Sec. 104]. Millions of billing and administrative jobs in the sector would shrink, with retraining priority offered [S3 Sec. 303(e)].

The program would negotiate prices annually, pursue bulk procurement, and run a formulary that steers prescribing toward generics, cutting into the prices and volume that brand-name drugs currently command [S3 Sec. 205].

industries.industry: For-profit hospitals and investor-owned care providers
industries.note: No investor-owned institution could participate; owners would be required to convert to nonprofit status over 15 years, compensated only for appraised real property and equipment, not lost business profits [S3 Sec. 103(a)].

industries.industry: Nonprofit hospitals, community health centers, and care-delivering nonprofit HMOs
industries.note: These providers would become the permanent channel for all American health care, paid through negotiated global budgets, capitation, and fee schedules set in consultation with provider representatives, with private insurers barred from competing on medically necessary care [S3 Sec. 103(c), 202].

industries.industry: Medical billing, claims processing, and health administrative services
industries.note: The bill's stated funding mechanism is 'vastly reducing paperwork', replacing thousands of private billing systems with one electronic system, eliminating jobs the bill would address only through retraining priority [S2][S3 Sec. 211(c), 303(e), 304].
